title: Alfalfa Sprout Outbreak Sickens 40 Across Minnesota and Wisconsin in Latest Food Safety Crisis
excerpt: E. coli and Salmonella linked to Everything Sprouts and Calco brands; health officials urge consumers to discard all affected products.
body:
• At least 40 people across Minnesota and Wisconsin have fallen ill from E. coli and Salmonella linked to alfalfa sprouts from the Everything Sprouts and Calco brands.
  • Three people have been hospitalized; health officials in both states are urging consumers to throw out any sprouts from these brands immediately.
  • The outbreak is part of a broader summer of food recalls across the U.S., including the record-breaking cyclosporiasis crisis tied to contaminated lettuce.
  • Sprouts remain a perennial food safety risk — the FDA has long warned vulnerable populations, including children and the elderly, to avoid raw sprouts entirely.

Health officials in Minnesota and Wisconsin are warning consumers to discard alfalfa sprouts from the Everything Sprouts and Calco brands after a multi-state outbreak of E. coli and Salmonella infections sickened at least 40 people.

Two States, Two Pathogens

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services confirmed on August 20 that 17 residents had fallen ill with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli and Salmonella linked to alfalfa sprouts. One person has been hospitalized. In Minnesota, health officials reported 23 cases between July 8 and August 8, with two hospitalizations. No deaths have been reported in either state.

The contaminated sprouts were produced by Everything Sprouts, a Minnesota-based grower, and distributed to restaurants and grocery stores under the Everything Sprouts and Calco brand names. State and federal investigators have not yet pinpointed the exact source of contamination.

\"People should refrain from eating alfalfa sprouts from the Everything Sprouts and Calco brands.\"

— Wisconsin Department of Health Services

A Summer of Food Safety Crises

The alfalfa sprout outbreak arrives amid what has been an unusually dangerous summer for foodborne illness in the United States. Wisconsin alone has recorded 270 cases of cyclosporiasis this year from contaminated lettuce, and the state has also identified 12 cases of Salmonella linked to jalapeno peppers sold at Chipotle Mexican Grill and Qdoba, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.

Nationally, the cyclosporiasis crisis has grown into one of the largest foodborne illness events in recent U.S. history, with the CDC reporting over 15,700 confirmed cases across 47 states as of August 17. That outbreak has been tied to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico, prompting a nationwide recall.

Why Sprouts Are a Recurring Risk

Alfalfa sprouts have been linked to foodborne illness outbreaks for decades. The warm, humid conditions required for sprouting create an ideal breeding ground for bacteria like E. coli and Salmonella. Seeds can become contaminated in the field, and once pathogens are present, the sprouting process can amplify them to dangerous levels before the product ever reaches a consumer.

The FDA has long advised that children, the elderly, pregnant women, and anyone with a weakened immune system should avoid eating raw sprouts of any kind. The agency recommends cooking sprouts thoroughly to reduce the risk of infection.

What Indian-American Consumers Should Know

Sprouts are a staple in many South Asian kitchens — mung bean sprouts in particular feature prominently in salads, chaats, and stir-fries. While this outbreak specifically involves alfalfa sprouts, food safety experts note that all raw sprouts carry inherent risks regardless of variety. Indian-American families accustomed to using sprouts in everyday cooking should ensure any sprouts they purchase are cooked thoroughly before consumption, especially when preparing meals for children or elderly family members.

Symptoms and Next Steps

Anyone who has eaten alfalfa sprouts from the implicated brands should monitor for symptoms. Shiga toxin-producing E. coli typically causes stomach cramps and diarrhea — often bloody — within two to five days of exposure. Salmonella symptoms, which include cramps, diarrhea, and fever, can emerge between six hours and six days after consumption.

Health officials from both states are working with the CDC, the FDA, and officials from other states to identify the full scope of the contamination. The Minnesota Department of Health has warned that the number of illnesses is likely to increase as the investigation continues.
